claim: Copy number alterations (CNAs) in cancer patients show a large variability in their number, length and position.
source: Copy number alterations (CNAs) in cancer patients show a large variability in their number, length and position, but the sources of this variability are not known.
evidence: This is stated as a known observation in the abstract.

claim: CNA number and length are linked to patient survival.
source: CNA number and length are linked to patient survival, suggesting clinical relevance.
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: CONIM proteins cluster into a densely connected subnetwork of physical interactions.
source: CONIM proteins cluster into a densely connected subnetwork of physical interactions and many of them are epigenetic modifiers.
evidence: Supported by network analysis showing 32 CONIM proteins connected via 42 physical interactions.

claim: Many CONIM proteins are epigenetic modifiers.
source: CONIM proteins cluster into a densely connected subnetwork of physical interactions and many of them are epigenetic modifiers.
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis showing enrichment of chromatin modification terms.

claim: The presence of heterochromatin in the tissue-of-origin contributes to the recurrence and length of CNAs in the respective cancer type.
source: We found that the presence of heterochromatin in the tissue-of-origin contributes to the recurrence and length of CNAs in the respective cancer type.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing enrichment of heterochromatin at CNA breakpoints and correlation between heterochromatin percentage and CNA properties.

claim: The epigenomic profile of the tissue-of-origin highly influences local mutation rates along the chromosome.
source: For point mutations, we are beginning to understand the determinants of this variation: the epigenomic profile of the tissue-of-origin highly influences local mutation rates along the chromosome (Schuster-Böckler and Lehner, 2012; Polak et al., 2015; Supek and Lehner, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different mutagens induce characteristic mutational signatures.
source: different mutagens induce characteristic mutational signatures (Alexandrov et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Tissue-specific exposure to environmental factors affects the selection of mutations during tumourigenesis.
source: tissue-specific exposure to environmental factors affects the selection of mutations during tumourigenesis (Schaefer and Serrano, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In the TCGA dataset used in this analysis, 59 genes on average are affected by a single CNA.
source: This is partly due to the fact that CNAs tend to affect several genes at the same time [in the dataset from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA; http://cancergenome.nih.gov/) used in this analysis, 59 genes on average are affected by a single CNA].
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data.

claim: Cancer samples usually carry on average 46 CNAs.
source: In addition, cancer samples usually carry a much lower number of CNAs (on average 46 CNAs in the patient samples considered in this study) than single nucleotide variants (SNVs; usually 10.000s per cancer genome).
evidence: Supported by analysis of patient samples in this study.

claim: Cancer samples usually carry 10,000s of single nucleotide variants per cancer genome.
source: In addition, cancer samples usually carry a much lower number of CNAs (on average 46 CNAs in the patient samples considered in this study) than single nucleotide variants (SNVs; usually 10.000s per cancer genome).
evidence: Stated as a known observation.

claim: CNA breakpoints are preferentially located in close proximity to DNA-methylation-depleted G-quadruplex sequences.
source: Authors have reported that CNA breakpoints are preferentially located in close proximity to DNA-methylation-depleted G-quadruplex sequences (De and Michor, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: CNAs that are close to telomeres are longer than those found in internal regions.
source: In addition, CNAs that are close to telomeres are longer than those found in internal regions.
evidence: Stated as a known observation from previous work.

claim: There are several different mechanisms of CNA generation.
source: This suggests that there are several different mechanisms of CNA generation (Zack et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from observations about CNA length differences and supported by citation.

claim: DNA contact points in genome-wide chromosome conformation capture (HiC) proximity maps are more likely to become CNA breakpoints.
source: It has also been observed that DNA contact points in genome-wide chromosome conformation capture (HiC) proximity maps are more likely to become CNA breakpoints.
evidence: Stated as a known observation from previous work.

claim: The length distribution of CNAs reflects chromosomal interactions.
source: Thus, the length distribution of CNAs reflects chromosomal interactions (Fudenberg et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: TP53 tends to be mutated in CNA-rich cancers.
source: The observation that certain genes tend to be mutated in CNA-rich (TP53 and SPOP [Ciriello et al., 2013; Boysen et al., 2015]) or CNA-poor (CTCF and ARID1A [Ciriello et al., 2013]) cancers implies that, besides epigenetic factors, the genetic background of the cell influences CNA variation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SPOP tends to be mutated in CNA-rich cancers.
source: The observation that certain genes tend to be mutated in CNA-rich (TP53 and SPOP [Ciriello et al., 2013; Boysen et al., 2015]) or CNA-poor (CTCF and ARID1A [Ciriello et al., 2013]) cancers implies that, besides epigenetic factors, the genetic background of the cell influences CNA variation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CTCF tends to be mutated in CNA-poor cancers.
source: The observation that certain genes tend to be mutated in CNA-rich (TP53 and SPOP [Ciriello et al., 2013; Boysen et al., 2015]) or CNA-poor (CTCF and ARID1A [Ciriello et al., 2013]) cancers implies that, besides epigenetic factors, the genetic background of the cell influences CNA variation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ARID1A tends to be mutated in CNA-poor cancers.
source: The observation that certain genes tend to be mutated in CNA-rich (TP53 and SPOP [Ciriello et al., 2013; Boysen et al., 2015]) or CNA-poor (CTCF and ARID1A [Ciriello et al., 2013]) cancers implies that, besides epigenetic factors, the genetic background of the cell influences CNA variation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The genetic background of the cell influences CNA variation.
source: The observation that certain genes tend to be mutated in CNA-rich (TP53 and SPOP [Ciriello et al., 2013; Boysen et al., 2015]) or CNA-poor (CTCF and ARID1A [Ciriello et al., 2013]) cancers implies that, besides epigenetic factors, the genetic background of the cell influences CNA variation.
evidence: Inferred from observations about gene mutations and CNA numbers.

claim: For five of the 19 cancer types (brca, lgg, hnsc, paad and ucec), fewer CNAs were significantly associated with a longer survival period (p < 0.05).
source: We observed that for five of the 19 cancer types (brca, lgg, hnsc, paad and ucec) for which we had CNA and survival data, fewer CNAs were significantly associated with a longer survival period (p < 0.05; chi-square test; see Figure 1B as an example).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In two out of the 19 cancer types (lgg and lihc), samples in the bottom quartile of the average CNA length were associated with a longer survival compared to samples from the top quartile (p < 0.05).
source: In addition, in two out of the 19 cancer types (lgg and lihc), samples in the bottom quartile of the average CNA length were associated with a longer survival compared to samples from the top quartile (p < 0.05; chi-square test; see Figure 1C as an example), again controlling for mutation number and ploidy.
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In none of the cancer types were fewer or shorter CNAs significantly associated with shorter survival.
source: In none of the cancer types were fewer or shorter CNAs significantly associated with shorter survival.
evidence: Supported by survival analysis results.

claim: 63 genes are associated with significantly different CNA numbers.
source: This resulted in a list of 63 genes that are associated with significantly different CNA numbers.
evidence: Supported by computational pipeline analysis of 5,734 samples from 20 cancer types.

claim: Mutations in 62 CONIM genes are associated with significantly fewer CNAs.
source: Mutations in 62 of these genes are associated with significantly fewer CNAs, whereas one gene (TP53) is associated with a significantly higher number of CNAs (see Supplementary file 1 for the full gene list and Figure 2A for two examples).
evidence: Supported by analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutations in TP53 are associated with a significantly higher number of CNAs.
source: Mutations in 62 of these genes are associated with significantly fewer CNAs, whereas one gene (TP53) is associated with a significantly higher number of CNAs (see Supplementary file 1 for the full gene list and Figure 2A for two examples).
evidence: Supported by analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 15 of the 63 CONIM genes are known to be frequently mutated in cancer.
source: Of the 63 CONIM genes, 15 are known to be frequently mutated in cancer (Lawrence et al., 2014), and as such are likely to be drivers of malignant transformation.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The fraction of frequently mutated cancer genes among CONIM genes is higher than expected by chance (p < e-16).
source: Their fraction among CONIM genes is higher than expected by chance (p < e-16; chi-square test).
evidence: Supported by statistical test.

claim: Mutations in CONIM genes have, on average, a stronger functional impact than those in genes not associated with a change in CNA number.
source: We found that mutations in CONIM genes have, on average, a stronger functional impact than those in genes not associated with a change in CNA number.
evidence: Supported by functional impact score analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In two out of five cancer types tested, mutations in CONIM genes were associated with a lower VAF.
source: We found that in two out of five cancer types tested, mutations in CONIM genes were associated with a lower VAF (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by VAF analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations in CONIM genes tend to arise later in time but are more likely to be pathogenic than those in genes having similar mutation frequencies.
source: This suggests that mutations in CONIM genes tend to arise later in time but are more likely to be pathogenic than those in genes having similar mutation frequencies.
evidence: Inferred from VAF and functional impact score analyses.

claim: Chromosome organisation is enriched among CONIM genes (q < e-4).
source: Among the most frequent GO terms were chromosome organisation (q < e-4; all functional enrichments FDR corrected) and chromatin modification (q < 0.001)
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chromatin modification is enriched among CONIM genes (q < 0.001).
source: Among the most frequent GO terms were chromosome organisation (q < e-4; all functional enrichments FDR corrected) and chromatin modification (q < 0.001)
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Eight CONIM genes were involved in histone modification (q < 0.001).
source: More specifically, eight CONIM genes were involved in histone modification (q < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Three CONIM genes were related to histone deacetylation (q < 0.01).
source: Of these, three genes were related to histone deacetylation (q < 0.01) and another three to histone methylation (q < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Three CONIM genes were related to histone methylation (q < 0.05).
source: Of these, three genes were related to histone deacetylation (q < 0.01) and another three to histone methylation (q < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis.

claim: 17 of the 63 CONIM genes had functions related to the structural organisation of the chromosomes or to epigenetic modifications.
source: Together, 17 of the 63 genes had functions related to the structural organisation of the chromosomes or to epigenetic modifications (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by functional annotation analysis.

claim: 'DNA Damage/Telomere Stress Induced Senescence' pathway is enriched among CONIM genes (q < 0.01).
source: Several pathways related to DNA damage were strongly enriched [e.g., 'DNA Damage/Telomere Stress Induced Senescence' (q < 0.01) and 'DNA Damage Response (only ATM dependent)' (q < e-4)].
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 'DNA Damage Response (only ATM dependent)' pathway is enriched among CONIM genes (q < e-4).
source: Several pathways related to DNA damage were strongly enriched [e.g., 'DNA Damage/Telomere Stress Induced Senescence' (q < 0.01) and 'DNA Damage Response (only ATM dependent)' (q < e-4)].
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The ATM DNA damage response plays an important role in the repair of double-stranded DNA breaks from which CNAs originate.
source: Notably, the ATM (Ataxia Telangiectasia Mutated) DNA damage response plays an important role in the repair of double-stranded DNA breaks from which CNAs originate.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about ATM function.

claim: TP53 is a member of both 'DNA Damage/Telomere Stress Induced Senescence' and 'DNA Damage Response (only ATM dependent)' pathways.
source: TP53 is a member of both pathways.
evidence: Stated based on pathway membership analysis.

claim: The greater number of CNAs in TP53-mutated samples might reflect the incapability of the affected cells to repair DNA breaks or to initiate apoptosis upon damage.
source: The greater number of CNAs in TP53-mutated samples might reflect the incapability of the affected cells to repair DNA breaks or to initiate apoptosis upon damage.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed association.

claim: 'Macromolecular complex binding' is enriched among CONIM genes (q < e-4).
source: Another group of the most strongly enriched terms centered on complex formation [e.g. 'macromolecular complex binding' (q < e-4) and 'macromolecular complex subunit organisation' (q < 0.001)].
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 'Macromolecular complex subunit organisation' is enriched among CONIM genes (q < 0.001).
source: Another group of the most strongly enriched terms centered on complex formation [e.g. 'macromolecular complex binding' (q < e-4) and 'macromolecular complex subunit organisation' (q < 0.001)].
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 540 genes are significantly associated with shorter or longer CNAs (FDR corrected q < 0.01).
source: We found 540 genes that are significantly associated with shorter or longer CNAs (FDR corrected q < 0.01; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Out of 540 genes associated with CNA length, 122 were also associated with a significantly different CNA number (FDR corrected q < 0.01).
source: Out of these 540 genes, 122 were also associated with a significantly different CNA number (FDR corrected q < 0.01; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test on pan-cancer set without applying any additional filters or corrections).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The overlap between genes associated with differential CNA length and those associated with differential CNA number was larger than expected by chance (p < e-16).
source: The overlap between the mutated genes found in samples with a differential CNA length and those found in samples with a differential CNA number was larger than expected by chance (p < e-16; chi-square test).
evidence: Supported by statistical test.

claim: 98.5% of genes associated with both CNA length and number were associated with fewer and shorter CNAs.
source: The majority (98.5%) of these genes were associated with fewer and shorter CNAs, suggesting that the same cellular mechanisms might influence both CNA number and length.
evidence: Supported by analysis of gene associations.

claim: The same cellular mechanisms might influence both CNA number and length.
source: The majority (98.5%) of these genes were associated with fewer and shorter CNAs, suggesting that the same cellular mechanisms might influence both CNA number and length.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that most genes affect both properties in the same direction.

claim: 32 of the CONIM proteins (50.8%) are part of a large connected network.
source: When linking CONIM proteins with protein-protein interaction (PPI) information [from HIPPIE version 1.8 (Schaefer et al., 2012)], we observed that 32 of the CONIM proteins (50.8%) are part of a large connected network (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by network analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The observed number of PPIs among CONIM proteins is significantly larger than in randomised networks (p = 0.001).
source: We found that both the observed numbers of PPIs (p = 0.001; randomisation test; Figure 3B) and the size of the largest connected component (p = 0.003; randomisation test; Figure 3C) were significantly larger in the original network than in the randomised networks.
evidence: Supported by network randomisation test shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The size of the largest connected component among CONIM proteins is significantly larger than in randomised networks (p = 0.003).
source: We found that both the observed numbers of PPIs (p = 0.001; randomisation test; Figure 3B) and the size of the largest connected component (p = 0.003; randomisation test; Figure 3C) were significantly larger in the original network than in the randomised networks.
evidence: Supported by network randomisation test shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CONIM proteins are enriched in the SWI/SNF complex (EP400, ARID1A, PBRM1 and ATRX).
source: In agreement with the functional enrichment, we found an enrichment of CONIM proteins in the SWI/SNF complex (EP400, ARID1A, PBRM1 and ATRX), which is involved in chromatin remodeling by restructuring nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by complex enrichment analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The SWI/SNF complex is involved in chromatin remodeling by restructuring nucleosomes.
source: In agreement with the functional enrichment, we found an enrichment of CONIM proteins in the SWI/SNF complex (EP400, ARID1A, PBRM1 and ATRX), which is involved in chromatin remodeling by restructuring nucleosomes.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about SWI/SNF complex function.

claim: Mutations in components of the SWI/SNF complex have been observed in different tumor types.
source: Mutations in components of the SWI/SNF complex have been observed in different tumor types, but their contribution to carcinogenesis is only poorly understood (Masliah-Planchon et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The contribution of SWI/SNF complex mutations to carcinogenesis is only poorly understood.
source: Mutations in components of the SWI/SNF complex have been observed in different tumor types, but their contribution to carcinogenesis is only poorly understood (Masliah-Planchon et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as current state of knowledge with citation.

claim: 1,036 unique CNA breakpoints are significantly more frequent in a certain cancer type than would be expected by chance (q < 0.1).
source: To this end, we assembled a list of recurrent CNAs (Mermel et al., 2011) that are significantly more frequent in a certain cancer type than would be expected by chance (q < 0.1; FDR corrected), resulting in 1,036 unique CNA breakpoints.
evidence: Supported by analysis of recurrent CNAs using GISTIC2 algorithm.

claim: 'Heterochromatin' chromatin state shows the strongest enrichment at CNA breakpoints in associated tissues (p = 0.009).
source: The strongest enrichment was observed for 'Heterochromatin' (p = 0.009; chi-square test).
evidence: Supported by chromatin state analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 'ZNF genes and repeats' chromatin state is significantly enriched at CNA breakpoints in associated tissues (p = 0.03).
source: The only other significantly enriched state is 'ZNF genes and repeats' (p = 0.03; chi-square test; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by chromatin state analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The frequency of 'ZNF genes and repeats' state at CNA breakpoints is more than five times lower than that of 'Heterochromatin'.
source: However, the frequency of this state at CNA breakpoints is more than five times lower than that of 'Heterochromatin'.
evidence: Supported by comparison of chromatin state frequencies.

claim: H3K9me3 shows the strongest enrichment at CNA breakpoints in associated tissues (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.001 for windows between 10 kb and 10 Mb).
source: As expected, we observed the strongest enrichment for H3K9me3 (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.001 for windows between 10 kb and 10 Mb; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by histone mark enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: H3K9me3 enrichment decreases with increasing distance from the CNA breakpoint.
source: This enrichment decreases with increasing distance from the CNA breakpoint, suggesting a colocalisation of H3K9me3 marks with recurrent breakpoints in the tissue-of-origin.
evidence: Supported by analysis of H3K9me3 enrichment at different window sizes shown in Figure 4B.

claim: H3K9me3 marks colocalise with recurrent breakpoints in the tissue-of-origin.
source: This enrichment decreases with increasing distance from the CNA breakpoint, suggesting a colocalisation of H3K9me3 marks with recurrent breakpoints in the tissue-of-origin.
evidence: Inferred from the distance-dependent enrichment pattern.

claim: CNAs with H3K9me3 enrichment in close proximity to the breakpoint were longer than CNAs originating from H3K9me3-depleted breakpoints (p = 0.001).
source: We found that CNAs with a H3K9me3 enrichment in close proximity to the breakpoint were longer than CNAs originating from H3K9me3-depleted breakpoints (p = 0.001; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Breakpoints in H3K9me3-enriched and H3K9me3-depleted genomic windows do not differ in their positions relative to the chromosome end (p = 0.8).
source: When comparing the positions relative to the chromosome end, we did not detect any differences between breakpoints in H3K9me3-enriched and H3K9me3-depleted genomic windows (p = 0.8; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The difference in CNA length distributions between H3K9me3-enriched and H3K9me3-depleted breakpoints remains significant when excluding breakpoints within 1 Mb or 10 Mb of chromosome ends (p < 0.005).
source: Additionally, we tested the effect of excluding breakpoints located within 1 Mb or 10 Mb of the chromosome ends. Both tests re-confirmed significant differences in the length distributions of the two CNA groups (p < 0.005; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with controlled conditions.

claim: The difference in CNA length distributions might suggest distinct mechanisms of generation that depend on the epigenetic features present at the position where the DNA breakpoint appears.
source: The difference in length distributions might suggest distinct mechanisms of generation that depend on the epigenetic features present at the position where the DNA breakpoint appears.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed length differences.

claim: ATRX, EP400 and NIPBL bind to H3K9me3 directly or form H3K9me3-binding complexes.
source: None of the CONIM proteins specifically methylates H3K9, but the CONIM proteins ATRX, EP400 and NIPBL bind to H3K9me3 directly or form H3K9me3-binding complexes (Eustermann et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2013; Oka et al., 2011; Vermeulen et al., 2010; Kunowska et al., 2015; Nikolov et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Non-silent mutations in ATRX, EP400 and NIPBL affect a greater proportion of samples in cancer types that show strong H3K9me3 enrichment (p < e-6).
source: We found that non-silent mutations in these genes affect a greater proportion of samples in cancer types (luad, lusc, lihc and skcm) that show a strong H3K9me3 enrichment (> 2-fold change in 10 kb windows around breakpoints; p < 0.05; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test) in their tissue-of-origin (p < e-6; chi-square test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The absolute correlation between total heterochromatin amount and expression of CONIM histone modifiers is significantly larger than that of non-CONIM genes (p < 0.05).
source: We found that the absolute correlation between total heterochromatin amount and expression of either CONIM histone modifiers or all CONIM genes is significantly larger than that of non-CONIM genes (p < 0.05 and p < e-5; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The absolute correlation between total heterochromatin amount and expression of all CONIM genes is significantly larger than that of non-CONIM genes (p < e-5).
source: We found that the absolute correlation between total heterochromatin amount and expression of either CONIM histone modifiers or all CONIM genes is significantly larger than that of non-CONIM genes (p < 0.05 and p < e-5; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CONIM genes are implicated in controlling the overall amount of heterochromatin under healthy conditions.
source: One possible explanation for this observation is that (under healthy conditions) CONIM genes are implicated in controlling the overall amount of heterochromatin.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the correlation between CONIM gene expression and heterochromatin amount.

claim: NIPBL showed the strongest absolute correlation (−0.53) between tissue-specific expression and amount of heterochromatin in the same tissue.
source: We decided to focus on NIPBL, the CONIM histone modifier that showed the strongest absolute correlation (−0.53) between tissue-specific expression and amount of heterochromatin in the same tissue.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis.

claim: NIPBL has been implicated in the developmental disorder Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS).
source: This gene has been implicated in the developmental disorder Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) (Krantz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Mutations in NIPBL have been associated with chromatin decompaction.
source: Mutations in NIPBL have been associated with chromatin decompaction and, indeed, mutations that are predicted to have a more severe effect on NIPBL exhibit a stronger effect on chromatin (Nolen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Mutations that are predicted to have a more severe effect on NIPBL exhibit a stronger effect on chromatin.
source: Mutations in NIPBL have been associated with chromatin decompaction and, indeed, mutations that are predicted to have a more severe effect on NIPBL exhibit a stronger effect on chromatin (Nolen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Missense mutations in the HEAT domain of NIPBL have a stronger effect on CNA number in cancers than do other missense mutations.
source: We therefore tested whether mutations in the HEAT domain, which is necessary to target NIPBL to sites of DNA damage (Oka et al., 2011), have a stronger effect on CNA number in cancers than do other missense mutations.
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cancers with truncating mutations in the N-terminus of NIPBL are associated with a significantly lower CNA number as compared to those with truncating mutations in the C-terminus.
source: We also checked whether cancers with truncating mutations in the N-terminus of NIPBL are associated with a significantly lower CNA number as compared to those with truncating mutations in the C-terminus (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The average number of CNAs per cancer type is correlated with the percentage of heterochromatin in the associated tissue (Spearman's rho = 0.72, p = 0.02, excluding ovarian cancer).
source: For most cancer types, we observed that the average number of CNAs is highly correlated to the percentage of heterochromatin in the associated tissue (Figure 5C). Ovarian cancer does not follow the general trend, but for other cancer types (for which we had CNA numbers and heterochromatin information available), we observed a Spearman correlation of 0.72 (p = 0.02).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The distribution of CNA numbers over cancer types is linked to the chromatin organisation of the tissue-of-origin.
source: This suggests that the distribution of CNA numbers over cancer types is linked to the chromatin organisation of the tissue-of-origin.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between CNA numbers and heterochromatin percentage.

claim: The mean length of CNAs for each cancer type is correlated with the percentage of heterochromatin in the tissue from which the cancer originated (Spearman's rho = 0.85, p = 0.002, excluding ovarian cancer).
source: Again, we observed a good correlation for most cancer types except for ovarian cancer (Spearman's rho = 0.85; p = 0.002), which decreases but remains significant when ovarian cancer is included (Spearman's rho = 0.62; p = 0.04; Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The correlation between mean CNA length and heterochromatin percentage remains significant when ovarian cancer is included (Spearman's rho = 0.62, p = 0.04).
source: Again, we observed a good correlation for most cancer types except for ovarian cancer (Spearman's rho = 0.85; p = 0.002), which decreases but remains significant when ovarian cancer is included (Spearman's rho = 0.62; p = 0.04; Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The altered activity of CONIM genes affects the amount of heterochromatin, with more heterochromatin leading to more and on average longer CNAs, and with less heterochromatin having the opposite effect.
source: These observations provide a possible explanation for how mutations in CONIM genes could affect CNA numbers and lengths: the altered activity of CONIM genes affects the amount of heterochromatin, with more heterochromatin leading to more and on average longer CNAs, and with less heterochromatin having the opposite effect.
evidence: Proposed mechanistic model based on multiple observations.

claim: The tissue-specific differences in CNA number seem to reflect the tissue-specific differences in heterochromatin.
source: The tissue-specific differences in CNA number seem to reflect the tissue-specific differences in heterochromatin.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between tissue-specific heterochromatin and CNA numbers.

claim: Only about 24% of CONIM genes have previously been associated with cancer.
source: They are characterised by being associated with the amount of chromosomal gain or loss in a cancer cell, but only about 24% of these genes have previously been associated with cancer.
evidence: Calculated from the 15 out of 63 CONIM genes known to be frequently mutated in cancer.

claim: Mutations in all but one of the CONIM genes are associated with a smaller number of CNAs.
source: Mutations in all but one of the CONIM genes are associated with a smaller number of CNAs.
evidence: Supported by the finding that 62 out of 63 CONIM genes are associated with fewer CNAs.

claim: Mutations in CONIM genes tend to occur late during cancer development.
source: One explanation for this observation could be that mutations in CONIM genes tend to occur late during cancer development.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observation that most CONIM genes are associated with fewer CNAs.

claim: Inactivation of TP53 decreases sensitivity to apoptosis.
source: Inactivation of TP53 decreases sensitivity to apoptosis, and therefore more DNA damage (including CNAs) is tolerated.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about TP53 function.

claim: An inverse relation between the number of CNAs and the number of point mutations has been described.
source: Previously, an inverse relation between the number of CNAs and the number of point mutations has been described (Ciriello et al., 2013), subdividing tumors into two groups: one CNA-rich and one mutation-rich.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The CNA-rich tumor group has been associated with recurrent mutations in TP53.
source: The CNA-rich group has been associated with recurrent mutations in TP53 and the mutation-rich (and CNA-depleted) group with mutations in ARID1A and CTCF.
evidence: Stated as a known observation from previous work.

claim: The mutation-rich (and CNA-depleted) tumor group has been associated with mutations in ARID1A and CTCF.
source: The CNA-rich group has been associated with recurrent mutations in TP53 and the mutation-rich (and CNA-depleted) group with mutations in ARID1A and CTCF.
evidence: Stated as a known observation from previous work.

claim: A higher number of CNAs has been reported in SPOP-mutated prostate cancer.
source: Several other studies investigated relations between point mutations and CNA numbers in single cancer types: a higher number of CNAs has been reported in SPOP-mutated prostate cancer (Boysen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Lower CNA numbers have been detected in CASP8-mutated oral squamous cell carcinoma.
source: Lower CNA numbers have been detected in CASP8-mutated oral squamous cell carcinoma (Pickering et al., 2013) and in CTNNB1-mutated endometrial cancer (Kandoth et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Lower CNA numbers have been detected in CTNNB1-mutated endometrial cancer.
source: Lower CNA numbers have been detected in CASP8-mutated oral squamous cell carcinoma (Pickering et al., 2013) and in CTNNB1-mutated endometrial cancer (Kandoth et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: SPOP did not pass the pan-cancer CNA enrichment filter criteria because the effect of SPOP on CNAs is highly cancer-type-specific.
source: Unlike CASP8 and CTNNB1, which are part of our CONIM list, SPOP did not pass our pan-cancer CNA enrichment filter criteria because the effect of SPOP on CNAs is highly cancer-type-specific.
evidence: Explanation for why SPOP was not in the main CONIM list.

claim: SPOP was recovered by the cancer-type-specific alternative detection pipeline.
source: However, SPOP was recovered by our cancer-type-specific alternative detection pipeline (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by alternative analysis.

claim: Samples with POLE mutations have higher point mutation counts as compared to randomly selected samples.
source: We can confirm that samples with POLE mutations have higher point mutation counts as compared to randomly selected samples (carrying mutations in genes with similar mutation frequencies as POLE).
evidence: Supported by analysis of POLE-mutated samples.

claim: POLE-mutated samples do not have a reduced number of CNAs.
source: However, we do not find a reduced number of CNAs in POLE mutated samples.
evidence: Supported by analysis of POLE-mutated samples.

claim: ATM is required for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in heterochromatic regions.
source: ATM is required for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in heterochromatic regions, a process which is characterised by slow repair kinetics (Goodarzi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ATM-mediated phosphorylation of KAP1 triggers local decondensation of heterochromatin and thereby facilitates efficient repair.
source: ATM-mediated phosphorylation of KAP1 (KRAB-associated protein 1) triggers local decondensation of heterochromatin and thereby facilitates efficient repair.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about ATM-KAP1 pathway.

claim: It is not only the amount of cellular heterochromatin but also the cell's ability to decondense it that is important.
source: This suggests that it is not only the amount of cellular heterochromatin but also the cell's ability to decondense it that is important.
evidence: Inferred from the role of ATM in heterochromatin decondensation during repair.

claim: Previous studies have suggested the involvement of chromatin formation in determining the distribution of CNAs.
source: Other studies have begun to investigate the causes of variation in the frequency of CNAs throughout the genome by comparing distributions of CNAs to those of genomic and epigenomic features (De and Michor, 2011; Fudenberg et al., 2011; Zack et al., 2013). These analyses have suggested, among other features, the involvement of chromatin formation in determining the distribution of CNAs.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: None of the previous studies have systematically compared tissue-of-origin chromatin conformation to cancer-type-specific recurrence of CNAs.
source: However, none of the previous studies have systematically compared tissue-of-origin chromatin conformation to cancer-type-specific recurrence of CNAs (in a similar manner as it has been done for epigenetic marks and point mutations [Polak et al., 2015]).
evidence: Stated as a gap in previous research.

claim: Not just the distribution of SNVs but also the CNA breakpoint distribution seem to be influenced by local chromatin structure.
source: Our study complements these previous efforts by showing that not just the distribution of SNVs but also the CNA breakpoint distribution seem to be influenced by local chromatin structure.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Density of chromatin determines where CNAs occur or persist.
source: In accordance with other studies, density of chromatin (for example, differences in mechanical forces or exposure to mutagens resulting from the localisation of dense chromatin at the nuclear periphery [Misteli, 2007]) determines where CNAs occur or persist (the high degree of condensation might hinder the detection and repair of DNA damage [Peterson and Côté, 2004]).
evidence: Interpretation based on current study and previous literature.

claim: The high degree of chromatin condensation might hinder the detection and repair of DNA damage.
source: In accordance with other studies, density of chromatin (for example, differences in mechanical forces or exposure to mutagens resulting from the localisation of dense chromatin at the nuclear periphery [Misteli, 2007]) determines where CNAs occur or persist (the high degree of condensation might hinder the detection and repair of DNA damage [Peterson and Côté, 2004]).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Properties of the tissue-of-origin contribute to the variability in the number, length and distribution of CNAs over cancer types.
source: These factors are governed by the properties of the tissue-of-origin (which contribute to the variability in the number, length and distribution of CNAs over cancer types) and could be influenced by abnormal activity of epigenetic modifiers through mutation or differential expression (contributing to the variation on the patient-level).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Abnormal activity of epigenetic modifiers through mutation or differential expression could contribute to the variation in CNAs on the patient-level.
source: These factors are governed by the properties of the tissue-of-origin (which contribute to the variability in the number, length and distribution of CNAs over cancer types) and could be influenced by abnormal activity of epigenetic modifiers through mutation or differential expression (contributing to the variation on the patient-level).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on study findings.

claim: CONIM genes encode rather more H3K9me3 'readers' than 'writers'.
source: With respect to possible mechanisms of heterochromatin formation interruption, it is worth mentioning that CONIM genes encode rather more H3K9me3 'readers' than 'writers'.
evidence: Observation from functional analysis of CONIM genes.

claim: The local epigenome impacts where a DNA breakpoint occurs.
source: Interestingly, we found that the local epigenome not only impacts where a DNA breakpoint occurs but also the length of the resulting CNAs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The local epigenome impacts the length of the resulting CNAs.
source: Interestingly, we found that the local epigenome not only impacts where a DNA breakpoint occurs but also the length of the resulting CNAs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The increased average length of CNAs from H3K9me3-enriched regions is probably due to the fact that a greater degree of packaging of the interphase genome into heterochromatin facilitates long-range contacts between distant parts of the DNA, which then serve as end points for CNAs.
source: This increased average length is probably due to the fact that a greater degree of packaging of the interphase genome into heterochromatin facilitates long-range contacts between distant parts of the DNA, which then serve as end points for CNAs.
evidence: Proposed mechanistic explanation for the observed length differences.

claim: This interpretation is in agreement with the observation that the chromatin shapes the length distribution of CNAs.
source: This interpretation is in agreement with the observation that the chromatin shapes the length distribution of CNAs (Fudenberg et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Telomeres form heterochromatin.
source: As telomeres in fact form heterochromatin (Blasco, 2007), our findings might explain the previously observed position-dependent length differences.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The findings about H3K9me3 and CNA length might explain the previously observed position-dependent length differences of CNAs near telomeres.
source: As telomeres in fact form heterochromatin (Blasco, 2007), our findings might explain the previously observed position-dependent length differences.
evidence: Inferred connection between current findings and previous observations.

claim: Ovarian cancer may not follow the same trend as other cancer types regarding the link between CNA properties and heterochromatin due to very high mutation fractions in TP53 (94%).
source: Regarding the link between cancer-type-specific CNA numbers or lengths and heterochromatin proportions in the corresponding tissue-of-origin, ovarian cancer may not follow the same trend as other cancer types due to very high mutation fractions in TP53 (94% [Lawrence et al., 2014]).
evidence: Proposed explanation for ovarian cancer outlier status, supported by citation.

claim: TP53 deficiency is strongly associated with high CNA numbers.
source: In accordance with previous studies (Ciriello et al., 2013), we show that TP53 deficiency is strongly associated with high CNA numbers.
evidence: Supported by current study findings and citation to previous study.

claim: CNA number and size are clinically relevant.
source: To this end, our study highlights several interesting candidate genes that could be valuable drug targets as our analyses suggest that CNA number and size are clinically relevant.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from survival analysis results.

claim: The epigenome impacts CNA occurrence in a tissue- and patient-specific manner.
source: In summary, our observations suggest that the epigenome impacts CNA occurrence in a tissue- and patient-specific manner.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple findings in the study.

claim: CNA breakpoints are overrepresented in heterochromatic regions.
source: CNA breakpoints are overrepresented in heterochromatic regions, so the epigenome of the tissue from which a cancer originates has a large impact on where CNAs arise during carcinogenesis.
evidence: Supported by chromatin state enrichment analysis.

claim: The epigenome of the tissue from which a cancer originates has a large impact on where CNAs arise during carcinogenesis.
source: CNA breakpoints are overrepresented in heterochromatic regions, so the epigenome of the tissue from which a cancer originates has a large impact on where CNAs arise during carcinogenesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the enrichment of heterochromatin at CNA breakpoints.

claim: The CONIM gene set is enriched in chromatin-modifying genes.
source: In addition, we identified genes in which mutations are associated with differential CNA number and length. Interestingly, this gene set is enriched in chromatin-modifying genes, which could suggest that these genes influence CNA properties through chromatin modifications.
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis.

claim: CONIM genes could influence CNA properties through chromatin modifications.
source: In addition, we identified genes in which mutations are associated with differential CNA number and length. Interestingly, this gene set is enriched in chromatin-modifying genes, which could suggest that these genes influence CNA properties through chromatin modifications.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on the enrichment of chromatin-modifying genes among CONIM genes.

claim: Cancer cells that have undergone whole genome duplications are associated with higher CNA rates.
source: It has been shown previously that cancer cells that have undergone whole genome duplications are associated with higher CNA rates (Zack et al., 2013) and poor prognosis (Dewhurst et al., 2014), thus we removed aneuploid samples.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Cancer cells that have undergone whole genome duplications are associated with poor prognosis.
source: It has been shown previously that cancer cells that have undergone whole genome duplications are associated with higher CNA rates (Zack et al., 2013) and poor prognosis (Dewhurst et al., 2014), thus we removed aneuploid samples.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: CNA numbers have been linked to mutation rate.
source: As CNA numbers have been linked to mutation rate (Ciriello et al., 2013), we additionally excluded highly mutated samples.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.
